entry.title: The Origins and Early Development of BSD Unix
entry.content:
Links: fosscomics.com | hacker news

In the late 1970s, Bill Joy and researchers at UC Berkeley created the Berkeley Software Distribution (BSD) by bundling a Pascal compiler, line editors, and other utilities as an add-on package for AT&T Unix. By distributing these tools at cost, Berkeley fostered a tradition of sharing that helped spread Unix throughout universities and research institutions.

Following the release of the expanded 2BSD distribution, the acquisition of a VAX computer at Berkeley led graduate student Ozalp Babaoglu and Bill Joy to add virtual memory support to Unix 32/V. Their work culminated in 3BSD in December 1979, drawing the interest of DARPA and laying the groundwork for Unix's widespread adoption in government-funded research.

entry.title: OpenSSH on musl-based Linux Distributions Vulnerable to Password Bypass
entry.content:
Links: sshhole.com | hacker news

OpenSSH installations running on musl libc—including Alpine, OpenWrt, and Buildroot—are vulnerable to a password bypass affecting accounts with no password (marked with '*' in /etc/shadow). When a password longer than 256 characters is provided, musl's crypt() function returns '*' due to a length limit in its SHA512 implementation, which OpenSSH incorrectly validates as a successful match.

The vulnerability specifically affects systems using musl that do not utilize PAM and have password authentication enabled. To mitigate this risk, users are advised to upgrade to OpenSSH 10.6p2 or disable password authentication in their SSH configuration.

entry.title: Go Security Team Advises on Mitigating CVE-2026-98432 Linux Kernel Flaw
entry.content:
Links: groups.google.com | lobsters | hacker news

The Go Security Team has issued guidance regarding CVE-2026-98432, a critical use-after-free vulnerability affecting IPv4 TCP connection handling in the Linux kernel that can allow remote code execution when Multipath TCP listeners are exposed. While upgrading to a patched kernel remains the definitive fix, Go 1.24 and later versions enable Multipath TCP by default for listen sockets on Linux, making programs potentially susceptible unless mitigated.

Developers can disable Multipath TCP globally at runtime using the "GODEBUG=multipathtcp=0" environment variable, at build time by adding "godebug multipathtcp=0" to a go.mod file, or explicitly per socket using Dialer and ListenConfig settings. However, the security team cautions that program-by-program mitigations are fragile and stresses that updating the kernel is the only complete remedy, noting that any future changes to Go's default behavior will be discussed publicly.

A global study published in PLOS Medicine estimates that snake envenoming causes between 274,000 and 513,000 deaths and at least 2.1 million envenomings worldwide each year. Using a geostatistical model that combines literature reviews with environmental and socioeconomic factors to adjust for severe under-reporting, the researchers concluded that the public health crisis is significantly larger than official health statistics indicate.

Sub-Saharan Africa bears the heaviest burden, accounting for 45% of global envenomings and fatalities, with rates nearly three times higher than those in south Asia. The findings also show that over 800,000 survivors suffer long-term physical disabilities annually, exacerbating poverty in vulnerable rural communities and underscoring the need for targeted antivenom stockpiling and improved healthcare access to meet World Health Organization reduction targets.

entry.title: Curl Accidentally Turing-Complete for Nine Months
entry.content:
Links: seriot.ch | lobsters | hacker news

Between versions 8.12 and 8.16, the command-line data transfer tool curl possessed features that made it accidentally Turing-complete under unbounded resource assumptions. Config files could slice variable values and recursively include other files without an explicit depth cap, enabling the utility to simulate any two-counter Minsky program.

Release 8.17.0 introduced a five-level include cap that broke this reduction by restricting file inclusion depth. Although real-world physical constraints such as stack limits and memory allocation restricted execution depth in practice, the behavior illustrated how unexpected computational capabilities can emerge from configuration parsers.
